newsitem.title: CANADA: Union agrees to restructuring of Canadian.
newsitem.headline: Union agrees to restructuring of Canadian.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp's largest union will take part in a restructuring program in an effort to save the financially troubled airline, published reports said on Friday.

Reports quoted Dave Ritchie, vice president of the 5,300-member International Association of Machinists & Aerospace Workers (IAM), as saying "the employees will share some of the pain" to help the company save C$180-million a year over the next four years.
Details of the restructuring plan, which includes a 10-percent wage cut, have yet to be finalized, Ritchie said.

The IAM presented management with a long list of suggestions on how to reduce costs at the air carrier's operating arm Canadian Airlines International Ltd, and the two sides were expected to meet today to decide on a course of action, reports said.
The decision by the IAM executive to support the restructuring brings the union alongside the 1,100-member Canadian Air Line Pilots Association, which has also recommended its members accept cuts.
The airline's four other unions have so far rejected the cuts.

The Canadian Auto Workers union said past attempts to save the airline, including five-percent wage roll-backs in 1992 and 1994 and a 17-percent payroll cut in 1995, prove that wage cuts are not the solution.
"We've been there, done that," CAW local 1990 president Anne Davidson said in a statement. "It's time for real solutions."

Canadian Airlines has been meeting with its six unions since Monday in an attempt to agree on restructuring plans and to reach a new collective agreement with the Canadian Union of Public Employees, which represents 2,600 flight attendants.
The flight attendants have been without a contract since December. The two sides indicated they were close to a deal after round-the-clock negotiations yesterday, reports said.

Airline workers held a rally Thursday to urge Prime Minister Jean Chretien, who was in Vancouver, to once again step in and save the airline. The federal government has said the airline must restructure its operations before any aid is considered.
